replacement: “Lise!” said her mother firmly, though she smiled as she said it.

“Are you telling the truth? Well, then, after such a confession I believe that you are sincere and good at heart. If you do not find happiness, always remember that you are on the right road, and try not to leave it. Above all, avoid falsehood, every kind of falsehood, especially falseness toward yourself. Watch your own deceitfulness and examine it every hour, every minute. Avoid scorn, toward others and toward yourself. What seems bad in you will grow purer simply because you see it in yourself. Avoid fear too, though fear is only the consequence of every sort of falsehood. Never be frightened by your own faint-heartedness in pursuing love. Do not be too frightened even by your evil actions. I am sorry I can say nothing more consoling to you, for love in action is a harsh and dreadful thing compared with love in dreams. Love in dreams is greedy for immediate action, quickly done and seen by all. People will even give their lives, if only the trial does not last long but is soon over, with everyone watching and applauding as if at a play. But active love is labor and endurance, and for some people, perhaps, a whole science. But I predict that just when you see with horror that, in spite of all your efforts, you are moving farther from your goal and not closer to it—at that very moment, I predict, you will reach it. You will see clearly the miraculous power of the Lord, who has loved you all along and has been guiding you in secret. Forgive me, I cannot stay longer with you. They are waiting for me. Goodbye.”
“She does not deserve to be loved. I have seen her naughtiness the whole time,” the elder said teasingly. “Why were you laughing at Alexey?”

The elder had been out of his cell for about twenty-five minutes. It was already past twelve-thirty, and Dmitri, the reason they had all gathered there, still had not appeared. He seemed almost forgotten, though, and when the elder came back in, he found his guests deep in lively conversation. Ivan and the two monks were doing most of the talking. Miüsov was trying to take part too, and quite eagerly, it seemed. But he had no luck at that either. He was plainly pushed into the background, and his remarks were ignored, which only made him more irritable. He had crossed swords with Ivan before, and he could not stand a certain offhandedness Ivan showed toward him.
